clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive skeletal ciliopathy defined by the triad of craniofacial anomalies (notably dolichocephaly from sagittal craniosynostosis), narrow thorax with skeletal changes, and ectodermal defects affecting hair, teeth, nails and skin.

Caused by biallelic variants in intraflagellar transport genes IFT122, WDR35 (IFT121), WDR19 (IFT144), IFT43 and IFT52, placing it firmly among the retrograde-transport ciliopathies and allelic with other short-rib thoracic dysplasias.
Ectodermal features are highly characteristic: sparse, fine, slow-growing hair, small widely spaced or microdont teeth with enamel defects, and short, dysplastic or brittle nails.
Skeletal manifestations include brachydactyly, short limbs, a narrow rib cage and disproportionate short stature, reflecting the shared ciliary defect with Jeune and short-rib polydactyly syndromes.
Progressive chronic kidney disease from nephronophthisis-like tubulointerstitial nephropathy is a major determinant of outcome and must be monitored lifelong.
Hepatic fibrosis with ductal plate malformation, retinal dystrophy and, in some children, developmental or intellectual involvement may also occur, mirroring other ciliopathies.
Facial dysmorphism typically includes frontal bossing, a wide forehead, epicanthic folds, telecanthus, a flat nasal bridge and full cheeks alongside the elongated skull.

Diagnosis rests on recognising the combined ectodermal-skeletal-craniofacial pattern and confirming a biallelic IFT gene variant; overlap with cranioectodermal features distinguishes it from isolated ectodermal dysplasias.
reference.pathophysiology: Cranioectodermal dysplasia is a skeletal ciliopathy resulting from biallelic variants in genes encoding components of the intraflagellar transport complex A (IFT-A) and its accessory proteins, chiefly IFT122, WDR35, WDR19, IFT43 and IFT52. These proteins mediate retrograde transport along the axoneme of the primary cilium, returning signalling molecules and structural components from the ciliary tip to the base. The primary cilium is central to several developmental signalling cascades, most importantly Hedgehog signalling, which patterns the skull, thorax, limbs and digits, and it is also indispensable to the specialised sensory and epithelial cilia of the kidney tubule, retina and biliary tree. Disruption of retrograde IFT impairs ciliary assembly and signalling, producing the craniosynostosis and dolichocephaly, the narrow thorax and short tubular bones, and the ectodermal derivatives of hair, teeth and nails that depend on ciliary-mediated developmental cues. In the kidney, ciliary dysfunction drives a nephronophthisis-like tubulointerstitial process leading to progressive renal impairment, while hepatic ciliopathy manifests as ductal plate malformation and fibrosis, and retinal photoreceptor cilium involvement causes dystrophy. The multisystem phenotype thus reflects the ubiquitous role of the primary cilium across ectodermal and mesodermal tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (chondroectodermal dysplasia with polydactyly and cardiac defects)
Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy and other short-rib thoracic dysplasias in the same ciliopathy spectrum
Isolated ectodermal dysplasias (hypohidrotic and hidrotic forms) lacking skeletal and renal disease
Nephronophthisis and related renal ciliopathies presenting with tubulointerstitial nephropathy
Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (metaphyseal dysplasia with fine sparse hair)
Bardet-Biedl syndrome and other multisystem ciliopathies with renal and retinal involvement
Syndromic craniosynostoses when the elongated skull dominates the presentation
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal radiographic survey documenting brachydactyly, rib and long-bone changes and craniosynostosis
Molecular genetic testing via a ciliopathy or ectodermal dysplasia gene panel, or exome/genome sequencing
Renal function assessment and renal ultrasound to detect and monitor nephronophthisis-like nephropathy
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for fibrosis and ductal plate malformation
Ophthalmological review including retinal examination and electroretinography for retinal dystrophy
Dental and orthodontic evaluation of enamel, tooth number and morphology
Cranial imaging and neurosurgical assessment where craniosynostosis affects skull growth or raises intracranial pressure
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure from craniosynostosis requiring neurosurgical assessment
Progressive decline in renal function heralding chronic kidney disease and eventual failure
Respiratory compromise in infancy from a narrow thorax
Evidence of hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension or synthetic dysfunction
Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty in a young child with the characteristic craniofacial and ectodermal features
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is dominated by the severity of renal and hepatic ciliopathy: progressive chronic kidney disease may culminate in end-stage renal failure, and hepatic fibrosis can contribute to morbidity. With multidisciplinary surveillance many children survive into later childhood and beyond, though outlook varies with the degree of visceral and thoracic involvement.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for an isolated ectodermal dysplasia and overlooking the skeletal, renal and hepatic ciliopathy that determine prognosis
Failing to institute lifelong renal surveillance, allowing nephronophthisis-like disease to progress unmonitored to end-stage failure
Overlooking silent craniosynostosis and the risk of raised intracranial pressure behind the dolichocephalic skull
Not recognising the shared ciliary basis and allelism with Jeune and short-rib polydactyly syndromes, delaying targeted genetic testing
Attributing short stature and dental anomalies to unrelated causes rather than the underlying ciliopathy
